section_summary: This section documents Japanese acquisition of strategic materials, foodstuffs, aircraft-related timber, and possible military supplies during the 1932 Sino-Japanese conflict. It includes official inquiries and export statistics showing that alleged United States Government arms sales were unfounded, alongside extensive consular reporting on Communist press claims that German firms were manufacturing and shipping ammunition, explosives, chemicals, communications equipment, and other matériel to Japan and the Far East. Departmental comments repeatedly note the political significance of these reports while questioning their reliability and asking consular officers to verify or condense them.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: report received by the League Council from the Shanghai Commission
subfiles.about: Cross-references a report received by the Council of the League from the Shanghai Commission.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a report from the Shanghai Commission to the League Council; report not reproduced.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 83: Mahogany shipment from British Honduras to Japan
subfiles.from: Robert M. Ott, American Vice Consul, Belize
subfiles.about: Reports E. Hirasawa's purchase of Belize mahogany for delivery to Japan and its intended use in airplane propellers.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 83: E. Hirasawa of Toa Kigyo arranged to buy about 50,000 square feet of British Honduras mahogany via Vancouver for March and April 1932, reportedly saying mahogany propellers suit military purposes better than metal.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Belize mahogany despatch to Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits the Belize consulate's report on a mahogany shipment to Japan for the ambassador's confidential information.
subfiles.summary: State forwards Belize Despatch 83 on the mahogany shipment to Japan to the Tokyo ambassador.

subfiles.title: Japanese purchasing of supplies in Mexico
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese purchases of Mexican cotton and seafood and inquiries concerning cattle exports.
subfiles.summary: Japanese interests are buying large quantities in Mexico, including cotton from Manzanillo and seafood; Arizona and Sonora cattle dealers want to sell steers to Japan; the Japanese mission asked about cattle.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Chinese rumor of a $180 million American munitions sale
subfiles.from: Consul General at Nanking, transmitted from Shanghai by Nelson T. Johnson
subfiles.about: Reports Chinese belief that the United States Government had sold $180 million in munitions to Japan and requests an authoritative denial.
subfiles.summary: A Chinese informant says many believe the US Government sold huge munitions to Japan, fueling resentment; the consul notes arms trade is private and asks an authoritative statement to rebut it.

subfiles.title: Departmental reply denying an American Government munitions sale
subfiles.about: Denies the alleged $180 million government arms sale and supplies actual American export figures.
subfiles.summary: Department says the alleged government sale has no basis: Commerce shows only about $12,000 of private firearms and ammunition exports to Japan in July-December 1931 and $2,000 in January 1932.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 48: German Communist reports of Japanese war-supply orders
subfiles.from: Frederic M. Sackett, American Embassy, Berlin
subfiles.about: Relays Communist reports of German production of machine-gun parts, military communications equipment, mortars, and poison gas for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Rote Fahne alleges Berlin-area factories make machine-gun springs, field telephones and mortar parts for Japan; Leuna Works Communists considered refusing a poison-gas order for Japan but continued because of unemployment.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Berlin Telegram No. 48
subfiles.about: Provides a paraphrased copy of the Berlin embassy's report on alleged German war production for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The paraphrase repeats Communist allegations concerning Germania-Reinickendorf, AEG Oberspree, Pintsch, and the Leuna Works. It records purported production of machine-gun springs, field communications equipment, mortar parts, and poison gas for Japan. The source also urged workers to resist manufacturing and transporting imperialist war supplies.

subfiles.title: Telephone memorandum on alleged United States Government munitions sales
subfiles.about: Records Major Crane's confirmation that no United States Government munitions sale to Japan had taken place.
subfiles.summary: Major Crane reports War and Navy officers agree claims of a recent US Government munitions sale to Japan have no factual basis.

subfiles.title: United States exports to China and Japan during January 1932
subfiles.from: Iron and Steel Division, Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce
subfiles.about: Tabulates January 1932 American exports of firearms, ammunition, aircraft, cotton, and nitrogenous materials to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Preliminary January 1932 table of US exports to China and Japan: very small firearms and ammunition to Japan, very large cotton shipments.

subfiles.title: United States exports to China and Japan during 1931
subfiles.from: Iron and Steel Division, Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce
subfiles.about: Tabulates calendar-year 1931 American exports of arms, aircraft, cotton, and nitrogenous materials to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Preliminary 1931 export table: cotton and aircraft-related goods greatly exceeded direct arms and ammunition exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1279: Purchase of foodstuffs by Japanese agents in Mexico
subfiles.from: J. Reuben Clark Jr., American Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Reports press accounts of Japanese agents buying Mexican foodstuffs for the Japanese army in China.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 1279: Mexican papers report Japanese agents buying beans in Jalisco and Zacatecas; contracts for shrimp, tomatoes, fish and chickpeas for forces in China through US firms and Japanese vessels.

subfiles.title: War Department inquiry concerning private sales of war materials to Japan
subfiles.from: Patrick J. Hurley, Secretary of War
subfiles.about: Asks the State Department's position on proposed private commercial sales of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The War Department had received inquiries from American businesses asking whether the government objected to sales of certain war materials to Japan. Hurley clarified that the prospective supplies belonged to private commercial interests rather than the War Department. Pages 21 and 22 preserve duplicate versions of the letter.

subfiles.title: State Department reply on private war-material sales
subfiles.from: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Patrick J. Hurley, Secretary of War
subfiles.about: Explains that private sales of war materials to Japan were lawful but asks to be informed of significant prospective transactions.
subfiles.summary: Stimson states that no legal prohibition prevented private persons from selling war materials to Japan and that the State Department therefore lacked authority to approve or disapprove such sales. He nevertheless requests notification of transactions whose quantity, character, or circumstances might affect American foreign relations.

subfiles.title: Military attaché report on Japanese purchases of German war materials
subfiles.from: Hugh W. Rowan, Assistant Military Attaché; forwarded for Edward Carpenter
subfiles.about: Comments on Communist newspaper allegations of German chemical and explosive production connected with Japanese orders.
subfiles.summary: Military attaché report on claims that German production of sodium nitrate, picrates, rayon and explosives reflected Japanese purchasing; Rowan cautions Communist sources are prejudiced but well informed; endorsement forwards it.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Japanese requirements for nonferrous metals
subfiles.about: Points to a letter discussing Japan's requirements for lead, copper, and zinc used in munitions.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Harold Hochschild's letter on Japanese demand for lead, copper and zinc, the three key nonferrous munitions metals.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: Japanese troop embarkation at Shanghai
subfiles.about: References Colonel Drysdale's report that Japanese troop embarkation would begin the following day.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Shanghai telegram with Colonel Drysdale's military report on planned Japanese troop embarkation beginning March 18.

subfiles.title: Colonel Drysdale's report on Japanese troop movements near Shanghai
subfiles.from: Colonel Drysdale, transmitted by Nelson T. Johnson
subfiles.to: War Department via Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese embarkation plans, front-line relief, aircraft patrols, and balloon observation.
subfiles.summary: Drysdale reports quiet fronts; Japan plans to embark the 24th Mixed Brigade and 11th Division, with the 14th taking their positions; Chinese object to Japanese aircraft beyond the patrol zone.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 593: Immense supplies of ammunition
subfiles.about: Transmits and translates a Communist article alleging major shipments of military chemicals, sulphur, and explosives through Hamburg.
subfiles.summary: The Süddeutsche Arbeiter-Zeitung alleged that ammonia, nitrogen, sulphur, acid drums, and millions of dynamite cartridges were moving through Hamburg toward Japan, China, or East Asia. It identified ships, sheds, forwarders, and purported destinations and urged transport and industrial workers to refuse participation. The German-language clipping is included after the translation.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 596: German manufacture and shipment of war supplies for Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards Communist press allegations concerning Bosch, German ammunition factories, Krupp, AEG, and Pintsch production for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Translated clippings alleged a large Bosch order for Tokyo, ammunition shipments from Karlsruhe, shell-ring production in Hamburg, and Japanese observation of Krupp gun trials. Further reports claimed that Berlin firms were producing machine-gun parts, field communications equipment, mortars, torpedo components, and shell fuses. Dominian considered the Communist paper fairly reliable for factory information, and the original German clippings accompany the translations.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 905: Shipments of war materials from Hamburg to the Far East
subfiles.from: John E. Kehl, American Consulate General, Hamburg
subfiles.about: Compiles translated Hamburger Volkszeitung reports of war-material production and shipments throughout Germany.
subfiles.summary: Kehl presents detailed Communist worker-correspondent reports covering explosives, ammunition, ammonia, grenades, poison gas, guns, telephone equipment, textiles, aircraft parts, and other matériel. The articles name numerous German factories, ports, ships, and alleged destinations in Japan, China, and the Far East. Kehl judges the reports fairly reliable as to commodity, quantity, and destination while treating their political interpretation with caution.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 606: Alleged Bosch order for trench lighting equipment
subfiles.about: Reports a rumor that Bosch was producing World War–type trench and dugout lighting equipment for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Dominian reports the Bosch magneto factory rumored to be working full capacity on a Japanese lighting-equipment order resembling German First World War trench systems.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 925: Further Hamburg reports of war-material shipments
subfiles.from: John E. Kehl, American Consulate General, Hamburg
subfiles.about: Presents further Communist newspaper reports of explosives, chemicals, ammunition, and aircraft parts shipped toward Japan and China.
subfiles.summary: The reports describe millions of dynamite cartridges marked for Japan, large ammonia and nitrate shipments, sulphur for Shanghai, and alleged grenade machinery and chemical production. They also discuss machine-gun and small-arms ammunition loaded under police supervision, American saltpetre purchases, and Japanese-bound shipments from Leuna and Adlershof. A separate notice records the annulment of Hugo Stoltzenberg's permission to manufacture chloracetophenone and store phosgene at Eidelstedt.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs note on the Hamburg reports
subfiles.about: Offers a brief, partly illegible assessment of the continuing Hamburg reports about German armament activity.
subfiles.summary: Handwritten Far Eastern Affairs reaction to the Hamburg reports on German armament restrictions and clandestine supply; largely illegible.

subfiles.title: Handwritten query concerning the series of reports
subfiles.about: Asks another official for an opinion on the continuing series of German war-supply reports.
subfiles.summary: Handwritten note observes the document is one of a series and asks what the recipient thinks of the reports.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 931: Continued reports of German war-material production and shipment
subfiles.from: John E. Kehl, American Consulate General, Hamburg
subfiles.about: Relays reports of German machinery, gun parts, explosives, chemicals, and other military supplies for Japan and neighboring states.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 931 compiles press reports of German production of bullet machinery, gun parts, explosives and chemical-warfare materials; Chinese firemen strike on the Coblenz and Hamburg dockworker action against war matériel.

subfiles.title: Confirmation of the Bosch trench-lighting order
subfiles.about: Reports corroborating evidence that Bosch was filling a Japanese order for 10,000 military lighting machines.
subfiles.summary: Dominian says the Bosch rumor appears confirmed by an urgent SKF Norma delivery of 20,000 ball-bearing sets, implying a Japanese order for about 10,000 machines.

subfiles.title: Division of Current Information comment on Communist press reports
subfiles.about: Recommends that Communist allegations be either verified or reported much more briefly.
subfiles.summary: Current Information sees no harm in reporting Communist press claims but finds the consular presentation vague and recommends verification or condensation.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 625: Reports of war-material shipments to the Far East
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese inspections and alleged shipments of ammonia, explosives, and Krupp guns from Germany.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 625: a Japanese commission reportedly inspected Leuna nitrogen plants; reports of ammonia from Alsdorf, explosives loaded at Duisburg for Japan, and Krupp guns tested near Löningen.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 939: Supplementary reports of German war-material production
subfiles.from: John E. Kehl, American Consulate General, Hamburg
subfiles.about: Compiles additional allegations of German production of barbed wire, uniforms, chemicals, ammunition, shells, and defensive equipment.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 939: Communist reports claim German firms produce barbed wire, ammonia, shells, phosgene and searchlights for Japan or others, with visits by military commissions, centered on Leuna and Bitterfeld.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 626: Reports of war production for the Far East
subfiles.doc_type: consular despatch with newspaper articles and translations
subfiles.about: Transmits two Communist articles and translations describing alleged German production and transport of war matériel.
subfiles.summary: The first article surveys barbed wire, ammonia, military clothing, shell rings, ammunition, and other supplies allegedly intended for Japan or the Far East and promotes an anti-war demonstration at Friedrichshafen. The second reports guarded ammunition loading at Lübeck, renewed powder production at Wittenberg, phosgene work at Ammendorf, convertible tracked vehicles at Breslau, and explosives and shells at Gelsenkirchen and Mülheim. Both German originals and English translations are included.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet: press criticism of Communist war-shipment reports
subfiles.about: Points to Despatch No. 942 concerning press criticism of Communist reports about war-material shipments to Japan and the Far East.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Hamburg despatch on non-Communist press comment on Communist articles alleging war-material shipments.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 942: National press comment on Communist war-shipment allegations
subfiles.doc_type: confidential consular despatch with translated article
subfiles.from: John E. Kehl, American Consulate General, Hamburg
subfiles.about: Translates a Hamburger Nachrichten attack on Communist worker correspondents and their disclosure of alleged German armament activity.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 942: a translated article accuses the German Communist Party of using worker-correspondents to publish false industrial information as daily high treason, tied to anti-war organizing; excerpt ends mid-passage.
